question_dict.context: A command and control behavior was blocked on host `vnevado-win10r`, which indicated an active infection by malware that could replicate and receive commands from remote attackers. This malware was active, and precautionary measures should be taken to check for residual signs of infection. The process involved had the ID 1332 and ran the command `curl http://vectorsandarrows.com`.
question_dict.question: What is the IP address associated with the Manatee Tempest activity group detected in this security incident?
solution: The account with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522` was involved in a Command and Control behavior that was blocked.
The cybercriminal group known as Manatee Tempest, which is associated with the IP address `198.43.121.209`, was active during the incident.

question_dict.context: A Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device at 2024-07-04 22:35:03.797541+00:00. Mimikatz is a tool used to harvest plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. The attacker might be leveraging this tool to harvest credentials to log into this or other devices on the network by impersonating a valid user. Several command line executions involving `mimikatz.exe` were observed, along with connected mimikatz-related files like `mimidrv.sys`, `mimispool.dll`, and `mimilove.exe`. More information can be found in the Mimikatz tool profile Threat Analytics report and the Actor profile: Storm-0875 Threat Analytics report provided by Microsoft.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]

•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

You need to answer a given security question by querying the database.

The attempt was carried out by the process `browsercore.exe` as observed from the process ID `2676`. Related to this alert, there was an active malware detected subsequently. Can you identify the name of the malware file detected on the machine?

execute[SHOW TABLES;]

<Thought>

- Process information
- Host information

- kiters.7z → kiters.7z.lockbit
- syncretic.7z → syncretic.7z.lockbit
- ponceau.7z → ponceau.7z.lockbit
- earlap.doc → earlap.doc.lockbit

Now let me search for alerts specifically related to the target device `vnevado-win11t` with AadDeviceId `e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033` to understand the initial ransomware payload launch.

Action: execute[SELECT * FROM SecurityAlert WHERE CompromisedEntity LIKE '%vnevado-win11t%' OR Entities LIKE '%e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033%' LIMIT 10]

tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

question_dict.question: What is the command line of the process that was executed when the 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected during lateral movement?
solution: The ransomware payload was remotely launched on the account `dp5hn` at `2024-07-04 22:35:01.951341+00:00`.

The 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected during lateral movement. The attacker's command line was `curl http://vectorsandarrows.com` and it was executed with Process ID `5572` on `2024-06-20t09:32:04.8002759z`.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]

•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. ('System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set default recoveryenabled no]', 'MDATP', 'Microsoft', '7d47542a-7c5a-4fd4-85f2-640f2bf0927b_1', '37ed1840-2428-9ace-8db4-fc7ceeda30b9', '', '', 'WindowsDefenderAtp', '', '', 'False', '2024-06-20 09:10:49.054537+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:10:51.876113+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:19:23.179872+00:00', '["1. Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.275880+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

This execution was flagged on 2024-07-04 at 22:35:03.869406+00:00 for its intent to dump user credentials. Subsequently, there was a lateral movement attempt to the jump server `Vnevado-jump` on 2024-07-10 at 11:24:45.260113+00:00. During this investigation, a potentially compromised user account was identified. Can you provide the SID of the user account that may be operating with ransomware-like behavior?

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

question_dict.context: A security incident regarding System recovery setting tampering and possible attempts to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was reported. Specifically, there was an attempt to disable system recovery features using `vssblatemp.exe` and `bcdedit` on the host `vnevado-win11u` with a user account having the SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522`. Notably, it included a potential access of PRTs, as mentioned in the Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report.
question_dict.question: In relation to the malicious credential theft tool execution detected in this multi-stage incident, can you identify the file name of the tool that was executed?
solution: The system recovery settings tampering was attempted by the user with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
An attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected, associated with the process `browsercore.exe`.
Another attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected, originating from the IP address `107.224.99.179`.
A malicious credential theft tool `mimikatz.exe` was executed.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

- LastIpAddress: 208.72.63.64

The "Suspicious remote activity" alert specifically mentions that the WMI commands were executed remotely. Looking at the evidence, I can see that the WmiPrvSE.exe process was the parent of the malicious commands. The key is to identify which IP was used to remotely execute these WMI commands.

From the network events I analyzed earlier, I saw that:
- vnevado-win10r had connections from 123.106.238.81 to port 135 (WMI) starting at 09:00:00
- vnevado-win10s had connections from 208.72.63.64 to port 135 (WMI) starting at 09:09:32

However, looking at the alert evidence more carefully, I notice that the "Suspicious remote activity" alert for vnevado-win10r shows IP 99.83.111.100 in the entities. Let me check if this is the actual source IP or if it's something else. Let me look more carefully at the network connections to understand which IP initiated the WMI commands.

Action: execute[SELECT RemoteIP, COUNT(*) as conn_count, MIN(Timestamp) as first_seen FROM DeviceNetworkEvents WHERE DeviceName IN ('vnevado-win10s.vnevado.alpineskihouse.co', 'vnevado-win10r.vnevado.alpineskihouse.co') AND Timestamp >= '2024-06-20 09:10:00' AND Timestamp <= '2024-06-20 09:11:00' AND RemotePort = '135.0' AND ActionType = 'ConnectionAcknowledged' GROUP BY RemoteIP ORDER BY first_seen]

Thought: Now I have a clearer picture. Looking at the WMI connections (port 135) during the attack window:
- 123.106.238.81 connected first at 09:10:21 (to vnevado-win10r)
- 208.72.63.64 connected at 09:10:47 (to vnevado-win10s)

Both IPs were used to remotely execute WMI commands on different machines. However, the question asks for THE IP address (singular) from which the ransomware payload was remotely launched. 

Looking at the timeline:
- 123.106.238.81 was the FIRST to connect and initiate the attack (at 09:10:21)
- The ransomware commands (bcdedit, vssadmin, etc.) started being executed shortly after

Let me verify which IP was associated with the initial attack by checking which machine received the first ransomware commands.

Thought: The first ransomware command was executed on vnevado-win10s at 09:10:48, followed by vnevado-win10r at 09:10:49. However, 123.106.238.81 connected to vnevado-win10r earlier (at 09:10:21), while 208.72.63.64 connected to vnevado-win10s at 09:10:47.

Looking at the security alerts, I can see that both machines were attacked, but I need to determine which IP was the primary source. Let me check the LastIpAddress field in the alerts more carefully. In the SecurityAlert data, I noticed:

For vnevado-win10s: "LastIpAddress":"208.72.63.64"
For vnevado-win10r: "LastIpAddress":"123.106.238.81"

These LastIpAddress values represent the IP addresses of the machines themselves (their internal IPs), not the attacker's IP. Let me look at the external IP addresses or check if there's a common source IP that orchestrated the attack across multiple machines.

Looking back at my earlier network analysis, 123.106.238.81 was the first to establish a WMI connection and had the most connections. This IP appears to be the primary attacker IP that remotely launched the ransomware payload.

- SHA256: 49a153e205875799ba3f9d26c69fe6ea1393376de0175cf458c1eae3a4a3b0de

During the security incident on device vnevado-win11t, three specific command lines were observed that indicate system recovery setting tampering:

1. bcdedit /set recoveryenabled no
2. bcdedit /set bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures
3. vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all

These commands were executed sequentially between 09:29:38 and 09:29:41 UTC on June 20, 2024, and are typical ransomware tactics to disable Windows recovery features and delete volume shadow copies to prevent system restoration.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures As per the recent alert, what is the name of the file that shows the potentially compromised assets exhibiting ransomware-like behavior?

- bcdedit /set recoveryenabled no
- bcdedit /set bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures
- vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all
- curl http://vectorsandarrows.com
- powershell -File C:Scriptsget-userprttoken.ps1

The WMI Provider Host (WmiPrvSE.exe) with this command line was used as the parent process to execute these malicious commands, which is a common technique used by malware to break the normal process tree and evade detection by making it difficult to trace back to the original malicious process that initiated the WMI calls.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

The process command used to tamper with the system recovery settings is:

**bcdedit /set recoveryenabled no**

This command disables the Windows recovery feature, preventing the system from automatically recovering from boot failures. This command was executed on multiple compromised devices including vnevado-win11t (where characterical.zip.lockbit was found) at 2024-06-20 09:29:38.

Additionally, a secondary recovery tampering command was also used:

**bcdedit /set bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures**

This command configures the system to ignore all boot failures and prevents the display of the Windows Error Recovery screen, further hindering recovery attempts.

Both commands were executed via WMI (wmiprvse.exe) as part of a LockBit ransomware attack originating from IP address 99.83.111.100. These commands are typical ransomware techniques used to prevent victims from restoring their systems through built-in Windows recovery features.

Action: submit[The process command used to tamper with the system recovery settings is:

**`bcdedit /set recoveryenabled no`**

This command disables the Windows recovery feature, preventing the system from automatically recovering from boot failures. This command was executed on multiple compromised devices including vnevado-win11t (where characterical.zip.lockbit was found) at 2024-06-20 09:29:38.

Additionally, a secondary recovery tampering command was also used:

**`bcdedit /set bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures`**

This command configures the system to ignore all boot failures and prevents the display of the Windows Error Recovery screen, further hindering recovery attempts.

Both commands were executed via WMI (wmiprvse.exe) as part of a LockBit ransomware attack originating from IP address 99.83.111.100. These commands are typical ransomware techniques used to prevent victims from restoring their systems through built-in Windows recovery features.]

has been detected. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

This actor, tracked by Microsoft and known to be a Russia-based cybercriminal group, has been active since June 2014 and is notorious for its Dridex banking trojan campaigns. Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Thought: Great! I found several ransomware-related alerts. I can see:
1. "File backups were deleted" alerts - indicating shadow copies and backups were deleted via vssblatemp.exe
2. "Manatee Tempest activity group" alerts - a known ransomware group

The alerts mention the user "dp5hn" (Grace Chen) and multiple devices (vnevado-win10s, vnevado-win10r, vnevado-win11u). Now I need to look for PsExec usage and find the actual ransomware file. Let me check DeviceProcessEvents for PsExec activity around the same timeframe.

Action: execute[SELECT * FROM DeviceProcessEvents WHERE (FileName LIKE '%psexec%' OR ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%psexec%') AND Timestamp >= '2024-06-20 09:00:00' AND Timestamp <= '2024-06-20 10:00:00' LIMIT 10]

Thought: No direct PsExec references found. Let me search more broadly for remote execution or WMI-based lateral movement, which is what I see in the alerts (wmiprvse.exe). Let me also look for file events that might show ransomware file creation or encryption activity. Let me check DeviceFileEvents for suspicious file activities around the time of the alerts.

Action: execute[SELECT * FROM DeviceFileEvents WHERE DeviceName IN ('vnevado-win10s', 'vnevado-win10r', 'vnevado-win11u') AND Timestamp >= '2024-06-20 09:00:00' AND Timestamp <= '2024-06-20 10:00:00' ORDER BY Timestamp LIMIT 20]

Action: execute[SELECT * FROM DeviceProcessEvents WHERE DeviceName IN ('vnevado-win10s', 'vnevado-win10r', 'vnevado-win11u') AND Timestamp >= '2024-06-20 09:00:00' AND Timestamp <= '2024-06-20 10:00:00' ORDER BY Timestamp LIMIT 20]

The logs are stored in a MySQL database, you can use SQL queries to retrieve entries as needed.
Note there are more than 20 tables in the database, so you may need to explore the schema or check example entries to understand the database structure.

The source IP address involved in this activity was `141.216.110.153`. During this incident, there have been numerous file system changes indicating possible ransomware activity. Can you determine the destination IP address where potential lateral movement was observed following the suspicious network event?

I'll help you investigate this security incident involving lateral movement and potential ransomware activity. Let me start by exploring the database structure and then trace the lateral movement.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.
